title: ARE CHRISTIAN INFLUENCERS MAKING DISCIPLES… OR JUST BUILDING PERSONAL BRANDS?
paragraphs: ARE CHRISTIAN INFLUENCERS MAKING DISCIPLES… OR JUST BUILDING PERSONAL BRANDS?

When Jesus becomes the content, followers become the currency, and ministry becomes a business, one terrifying question remains: Are we leading people to the Cross… or teaching them to admire the person holding the microphone?
Imagine standing before Jesus Christ one day.
Not as a content creator. Not as a pastor. Not as an author, worship leader, evangelist, or Christian influencer.
Just you.
No camera. No audience. No verified badge. No impressive ministry statistics.
And imagine having to confront a question you spent your entire online life avoiding.
“You told thousands of people about Me. But did you teach them to follow Me… or to depend on you?”
Now, those are not recorded words of Jesus. Scripture does not give us that exact conversation.
But the question behind them is frighteningly biblical.
Because Jesus once warned that not everyone who calls Him “Lord, Lord” will enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 7:21–23).
And that warning was not directed only toward people who openly rejected God.
It included people who claimed to have prophesied, driven out demons, and performed mighty works in His name.
Read that again.
People who could point to impressive religious activity.
People who could say they had done extraordinary things.
Yet Jesus exposed the terrible possibility that public ministry and genuine obedience are not always the same thing.
And perhaps that is where our conversation needs to begin.
Not with another attack on Christian influencers.
Not with another cynical declaration that every online ministry is a scam.
But with something much more uncomfortable.
What if the greatest danger facing Christian influence today is not that people have stopped talking about Jesus?
What if it is that we have become exceptionally good at talking about Jesus while quietly learning how to make everything revolve around ourselves?
And before anyone points a finger at somebody else, there is something we need to admit.
This temptation does not belong exclusively to famous preachers or creators with millions of followers.
It can live inside the person with fifty followers.
Inside the church volunteer who secretly resents not being recognized.
Inside the worship leader who feels disappointed when someone else receives the applause.
Inside the believer who shares Scripture but keeps checking how many people reacted.
And yes, it can live inside a ministry like Gospel Warrior too.
Nobody who speaks publicly about Christ is automatically immune.
Not even the person writing these words.
That is what makes this conversation necessary.
Because sometimes the most dangerous idol in Christian ministry is not money.
It is the version of ourselves that we have convinced people to admire.
And an idol becomes especially difficult to recognize when it is holding a Bible.
Jesus understood the human appetite for recognition long before algorithms existed.
In Matthew 6:1, He warned against practicing righteousness before others in order to be seen by them.
The Greek expression is πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι αὐτοῖς (pros to theathēnai autois).
It conveys the purpose of being seen or observed by others.
Notice what Jesus was exposing.
Not merely the fact that someone performed a good deed publicly.
But the motive behind it.
The desire to turn obedience into a performance.
The desire to make holiness an advertisement for oneself.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because public faithfulness is not inherently hypocrisy.
Jesus also told His disciples to let their light shine before others so that people would see their good works and glorify their Father in heaven (Matthew 5:16).
The difference is not simply whether people see you.
It is who receives the glory when they do.
One person shares a testimony because someone desperately needs hope.
Another shares a testimony because being admired has become emotionally necessary.
One person teaches Scripture because the truth has transformed their life.
Another gradually discovers that controversy, outrage, and dramatic declarations generate more engagement than careful biblical teaching.
And the terrifying thing is that, from the outside, both may look almost identical.
Both may quote Scripture.
Both may pray publicly.
Both may speak passionately about salvation.
Both may attract thousands of followers.
Only God sees the heart perfectly.
And sometimes, by His grace, He allows us to recognize what is happening inside our own hearts before our public success becomes our private destruction.
There is a story in Scripture that should make every Christian communicator tremble.
In John 3, John the Baptist's disciples came to him concerned that people were going to Jesus.
Think about the situation.
John had been preaching repentance.
He had baptized crowds.
He had faithfully prepared people for the coming Messiah.
Now attention was moving away from him.
The very people who once gathered around his ministry were turning toward Someone else.
In the world of modern influence, we might call that a devastating loss of audience.
But John did not panic.
He did not launch a campaign to reclaim attention.
He did not treat Jesus as competition.
Instead, he said something that may be the most important sentence any Christian influencer could ever learn.
ἐκεῖνον δεῖ αὐξάνειν, ἐμὲ δὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι.
Ekeinon dei auxanein, eme de elattousthai.
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
— John 3:30
The Greek word δεῖ (dei) expresses necessity: something that must happen.
John was not merely expressing a preference.
He understood that the growing prominence of Jesus was the very purpose of his own ministry.
His joy was not threatened when people went to Christ.
His joy was fulfilled.
Can we say the same?

Would we rejoice if someone stopped watching our videos because they had become deeply rooted in Scripture, committed to a healthy local church, and mature enough to walk with Christ without depending on our daily posts?
Would we celebrate if a person we discipled grew beyond us?
Would we be grateful if another ministry reached people we could not reach?
Or would some hidden part of us feel abandoned?
That is a painful question.
Because discipleship is not about creating lifelong dependence on the discipler.
It is about helping people become faithful followers of Jesus.
A true disciple-maker should be able to say, “I am thankful you listened to me. But I am even more thankful that you have learned to listen to Christ through His Word.”
And that brings us to something deeply troubling about the culture we live in.
We have learned to measure influence with numbers.
Views.
Likes.
Shares.
Comments.
Monthly revenue.
Audience growth.
Engagement rates.
And none of those numbers is automatically sinful.
A widely shared Gospel message may reach a person who would never enter a church building.
A Christian author may rightly receive payment for honest labor.
Paul taught that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from the Gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14), even though he sometimes chose not to exercise that right.
Financial support is not the enemy of faithful ministry.
But there is a difference between using resources to serve the Gospel and using the Gospel to acquire resources.
There is a difference between reaching more people because you love them and loving people primarily because reaching them increases your numbers.
And there is a difference between making disciples and manufacturing customers who are afraid to leave.
The Bible does not condemn every form of financial support for Christian ministry.
But it does condemn greed, manipulation, and treating godliness as a means of gain.
In 1 Peter 5:2–3, church elders are instructed to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for shameful gain, and not by domineering over those entrusted to them.
In 2 Corinthians 2:17, Paul distinguishes his ministry from those who peddle God's word for profit.
These passages do not establish that every paid ministry is corrupt.
They establish something far more searching.
The way we handle people, money, and authority reveals something about what we believe ministry is for.
And if a Christian influencer cannot be questioned without immediately accusing the questioner of attacking God's anointed, something has gone wrong.
If every criticism becomes persecution, accountability disappears.
If every disagreement becomes rebellion, the personality becomes untouchable.
If every financial appeal suggests that refusing to give means refusing God, generosity has been replaced with pressure.
Jesus did not commission His followers to build spiritual empires around personalities.
He commanded them to make disciples.
Matthew 28:19 begins with the Greek:
μαθητεύσατε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη
Mathēteusate panta ta ethnē.
“Make disciples of all nations.”
The key verb, μαθητεύσατε (mathēteusate), means to make disciples.
And Jesus immediately explains what that mission involves: baptizing people in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything He commanded.
That is much deeper than generating religious excitement.
A disciple is not simply someone who enjoyed your message.
Not simply someone who agrees with your opinion.
Not someone who types “Amen” and continues living as though Christ has no authority over their life.
A disciple is a learner and follower of Jesus, called to trust Him, obey Him, and grow in His likeness.
And that transformation cannot be reduced to analytics.
You can have a million followers and still fail to teach people what Jesus commanded.
You can have a small audience and faithfully help people understand the Scriptures, repent of sin, love their neighbors, persevere in suffering, and remain rooted in Christ.
Numbers can tell us how far content travels.
They cannot, by themselves, tell us how deeply the Gospel has taken root.
Think about that lonely believer who has been struggling for months.
The one who smiles at church but cries in the bathroom.
The one who has fallen into the same sin again and is beginning to wonder whether repentance is still possible.
The one who has prayed for healing, watched other people celebrate answered prayers, and quietly asked God why their own suffering continues.
Imagine that person opening Facebook at two in the morning.
They find a Christian video.
The music is beautiful.
The speaker is confident.
The editing is cinematic.
The comments are filled with declarations of victory.
But the message leaves them with one conclusion.
“If I had stronger faith, I would already be successful, healed, wealthy, or free from suffering.”
So they close the app feeling even more ashamed.
That is not what biblical discipleship should produce.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that sufficiently spiritual people will never struggle.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners, that He died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
It is the announcement that salvation is by grace through faith, not a reward for impressive religious performance (Ephesians 2:8–9).
It is the announcement that those who belong to Christ can bring their failures into the light, confess their sins, and find forgiveness and cleansing in Him (1 John 1:9).
And it is the announcement that following Jesus may involve suffering, self-denial, endurance, and a cross.
Jesus never promised that discipleship would make us celebrities.
He said:
“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.”
— Luke 9:23, ESV
Daily.
Not just when the camera is recording.
Not just when the post performs well.
Not just when the ministry receives financial support.
Daily.
When nobody applauds.
When telling the truth costs you followers.
When correcting a mistake damages your image.
When a struggling believer needs compassion instead of a motivational slogan.
When repentance requires admitting publicly that you were wrong.
When obedience is expensive and nobody notices.
That is where the difference between a personal brand and a life surrendered to Jesus begins to become visible.
And there is another biblical story we cannot ignore.
In Acts 8, Simon had amazed people in Samaria with his magic, and people regarded him as someone great.
Then Philip proclaimed Christ, and many believed.
Later, Simon saw the apostles laying hands on believers, who received the Holy Spirit.
And Simon offered money for the power he had witnessed.
Peter rebuked him sharply.
Why?
Because Simon attempted to obtain God's gift through money and revealed a heart that was not right before God.
Its immediate concern is the attempted purchase of spiritual power.
But it reveals a principle that should still disturb us.
Holy things must never become instruments of personal ambition.
The power of God is not merchandise.
The Holy Spirit is not a product.
Spiritual authority is not something we purchase, package, or possess for self-exaltation.
And human souls are not inventory.
There is a reason Paul asked the Corinthians:
“Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?”
— 1 Corinthians 1:13, ESV
The church in Corinth was struggling with divisions around human leaders.
Some identified themselves with Paul.
Others with Apollos.
Others with Cephas.
And Paul redirected their attention to the One who was actually crucified for them.
Christ.
Not Paul.
Not Apollos.
Not the most eloquent speaker.
Not the most admired religious personality.
Christ.
Imagine if we applied that question to our modern Christian culture.
Was your favorite influencer crucified for you?
Did your favorite preacher carry your sins on the Cross?
Did your favorite author rise from the dead?
Can your favorite ministry forgive your sins?
No.
Only Jesus saves.
And every faithful Christian voice, including this one, must remain willing to be measured against that truth.
But perhaps you are reading this as someone who has been hurt by Christian leaders.
Maybe you once trusted a ministry.
You gave.
You served.
You defended its leaders.
You believed their promises.
And then something happened.
Perhaps you discovered dishonesty.
Perhaps your questions were dismissed.
Perhaps you were made to feel guilty for not giving more.
Perhaps someone used Scripture to control you instead of helping you understand it.
And now, every time you see another Christian influencer speaking passionately into a camera, something inside you tightens.
You wonder whether the tears are real.
Whether the compassion is genuine.
Whether the message is simply another carefully constructed strategy to get your attention and eventually your money.
If that is where you are, your questions deserve to be taken seriously.
But please do not confuse the failures of people who represent Jesus with the character of Jesus Himself.
He is not another religious celebrity protecting His reputation.
He is the Savior who confronted hypocrisy, welcomed repentant sinners, washed His disciples' feet, and gave His life for His sheep.
He did not exploit the wounded.
He moved toward them.
He did not need to manufacture a scandal to gain attention.
He entered our broken world and bore the shame of the Cross.
He did not offer forgiveness as a premium benefit for those who could afford it.
He gave Himself for sinners who could never purchase their own redemption.
And here is where the Gospel becomes personal.
Because the Cross does not merely expose corrupt religious influence.
It exposes our own hunger to be important.
Our desire to be seen.
Our need to be affirmed.
Our tendency to turn even good things into ways of proving our worth.
The Gospel confronts that hunger with a Savior who had every right to receive honor yet humbled Himself.
Philippians 2:5–8 describes Christ's humility, culminating in His obedience to death on a cross.
The passage does not teach that Jesus stopped being divine.
It reveals the astonishing humility of the Son who took the form of a servant.
And that changes the way Christian influence should look.
If our Lord served, how can we justify using people?
If our Lord humbled Himself, how can we make self-exaltation our ministry strategy?
If our Lord gave His life, how can we treat wounded people as disposable engagement?
If our Lord told the truth even when people walked away, how can we compromise Scripture simply to preserve our audience?
The answer is not that Christian influencers should stop creating content.
The answer is that every Christian platform must remain under the lordship of Christ.
A camera can become a tool of discipleship.
A Facebook page can become a place where someone first encounters biblical truth.
A book can help a believer understand Scripture.
A video can encourage someone to seek help, confess sin, return to a local church, or begin reading the Bible.
An online ministry can serve people who are isolated, searching, grieving, or spiritually hungry.
These things matter.
But they must lead somewhere beyond themselves.
Toward Scripture.
Toward prayer.
Toward repentance and faith.
Toward fellowship with other believers.
Toward love expressed in real life.
Toward obedience to Jesus.
And toward the recognition that no digital ministry, however helpful, can replace the whole life of the church.
A faithful influencer should not fear a follower becoming spiritually mature enough to disagree with them respectfully.
A faithful ministry should welcome correction when it has misunderstood Scripture.
A faithful teacher should be able to say, “I do not know,” rather than inventing certainty.
A faithful Christian communicator should care more about whether a message is true than whether it is viral.
And a faithful audience should test what it hears.
Acts 17:11 commends the Bereans for examining the Scriptures to see whether Paul's teaching was true.
Think about that.
Even the apostle Paul's preaching was examined against Scripture.
How much more should our favorite online personalities be examined?
Do not surrender your discernment because someone has a large following.
Do not assume that emotional music proves biblical accuracy.
Do not mistake confidence for spiritual maturity.
Do not confuse expensive production with God's approval.
And do not automatically condemn a ministry simply because it has resources, sells books, or receives voluntary support.
Look at its teaching.
Look at its handling of Scripture.
Look at how it treats people.
Look at whether its leaders welcome accountability.
Look at what happens when someone says no.
Look at whether the ministry continually points beyond itself to Jesus.
Because a genuine servant of Christ does not need to become the center of your spiritual universe.
Jesus is enough.
And perhaps this is the question that should stay with every person reading this:
If the name of the influencer disappeared tomorrow, would the people they reached still know how to follow Jesus?
Would they still open their Bibles?
Would they still pray?
Would they still gather with believers?
Would they still seek holiness?
Would they still love their enemies?
Would they still trust Christ when life became painful?
Would they still know that forgiveness comes through Jesus rather than through loyalty to a personality?
If the answer is yes, something beautiful may have happened.
The messenger became less necessary because the message had taken root.
The servant stepped aside because people had learned to follow the Master.
And that is not a failure of influence.
That is one of its greatest possible fruits.
Now, I want to speak directly to the person who feels convicted.
Maybe you are building a ministry, and somewhere along the way, the numbers began controlling your emotions.
You started measuring your worth by the reach of your posts.
You became jealous when someone else succeeded.
You found yourself softening difficult biblical truths because you feared losing support.
You began enjoying the attention more than the responsibility.
Or maybe you are not a creator at all.
Maybe you have become more loyal to a Christian personality than to the Word of God.
Maybe you defend everything your favorite leader says without examining Scripture.
Maybe you spend hours watching Christian content but rarely spend quiet time with Jesus.
Maybe you know the opinions of your favorite preacher better than you know the teachings of Christ.
There is still grace for repentance.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Jesus does not expose our sin merely to leave us drowning in shame.
He calls us to turn from it and come to Him.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated “repentance,” refers to a change of mind or heart that, in biblical context, involves turning toward God and away from sin.
Repentance is not simply feeling embarrassed because someone discovered our motives.
It is acknowledging what is wrong and turning to Christ.
It is surrendering what we have been protecting.
It is saying, “Lord, even this ministry belongs to You.”
“Even this platform belongs to You.”
“Even this reputation belongs to You.”
“Even my desire to be remembered must bow before You.”
And if you have fallen, the answer is not to construct a more convincing spiritual image.
The answer is to come honestly to Jesus.
Because He does not need the polished version of your story.
He already knows the truth.
The failures.
The compromises.
The envy.
The hidden pride.
The secret exhaustion.
The prayers you stopped praying.
The motives you have been afraid to examine.
And the same Christ who calls sinners to repentance also offers forgiveness through His finished work.
That is why the words From Scandal to Grace matter so deeply to us at Gospel Warrior.
Not because every scandal should be excused.
Not because repentance removes every earthly consequence.
Not because a disgraced leader must automatically be restored to public ministry.
And certainly not because grace gives anyone permission to exploit people.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem sinners, transform lives, and bring truth and hope into places marked by shame.
Grace does not make accountability unnecessary.
Grace teaches us to stop hiding from the truth.
And genuine restoration must never come at the expense of those who have been harmed.
The Cross tells us both that sin is serious and that God's mercy is astonishing.
That is the Gospel we want to keep proclaiming.
Not a Gospel that makes Gospel Warrior famous.
Not a Gospel that makes any founder, writer, or creator indispensable.
But the Gospel of Jesus Christ, crucified and risen.
And this is also why we want to be transparent about the invitation we are making.
Gospel Warrior is committed to sharing Scripture-centered encouragement, biblical teaching, and discipleship resources.
At the same time, producing, maintaining, and expanding ministry resources involves real work and real costs.
It does not make you a better Christian.
It does not secure forgiveness or spiritual blessing.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing and not compelled.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says, God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we make this invitation.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
The heart remains Jesus.
The Word remains our foundation.
Discipleship remains our calling.
Not because we need another impressive number.
But because someone in your circle may be struggling with disillusionment toward Christian leadership.
Someone may be confusing religious popularity with spiritual authority.
Someone may have walked away from Christian community because a leader failed them.
Someone may be serving God publicly while privately losing the joy of knowing Him.
And someone may need to hear that Jesus is still worthy of their trust, even when the people who speak about Him are imperfect.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to start a public fight.
But to open a conversation that could lead to humility, healing, and renewed faithfulness.
And please, do not leave this article without examining your own heart.
I want to ask you something, and I hope you will answer with spiritual honesty rather than a polished religious response.
Have you ever found yourself admiring a Christian personality more than actually spending time with Jesus?
Or have you ever felt hurt, manipulated, or disappointed by someone who claimed to represent Him?
And if you want to share your experience, your testimony, or a Scripture that has helped you discern faithful Christian teaching, the comments are open for that conversation too.
You do not have to reveal private wounds or name individuals publicly.
But your honest words may help another believer realize they are not alone.
Because pride rarely announces its arrival.
Sometimes it simply begins by making applause feel necessary.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, struggling Christians, and even those who are still searching for truth to follow along.
Not because every question has an easy answer.
But because Jesus deserves to be sought with honesty.
And before we finish, I want to return to that opening image.
Standing before Christ.
No audience.
No camera.
No analytics.
No carefully written biography.
Only the truth of a life laid bare before the Lord.
Scripture teaches that believers will give an account to God, and that our works will be tested (Romans 14:12; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15).
But our hope of salvation does not rest in producing a perfect ministry record.
It rests in Jesus Christ, whose death and resurrection are sufficient for all who trust in Him.
That is why we must not build our identity on how many people know our names.
Our deepest joy is that, through Christ, we may belong to God.
The world may remember a Christian influencer for their charisma.
For their voice.
For their content.
For their success.
For their controversy.
But the greatest legacy any Christian communicator can leave is not an audience that cannot stop talking about them.
It is people who have learned to love, trust, and obey Jesus.
So let the platforms be useful.
Let the books be written.
Let the videos be made.
Let the resources reach people.
Let generous supporters help faithful ministries continue their work.
Jesus Christ is the Savior. We are not.
And when our names are forgotten, when the algorithms have moved on, when the applause has gone silent, may the people we served still be walking with Him.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be losing our audience.
It would be gaining the world's attention while forgetting the One we were supposed to proclaim.
May they forget the sound of our voices long before they forget the Savior we pointed them toward.
